extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, newsroom staff, and readers interested in media accountability
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for how a major newsroom should handle factual errors, complex disputes of news judgment and fairness, and the use of corrections versus editor's notes. Focuses on timeliness, transparency, verification, and procedures for accepting and publicizing fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction for factual errors
rubrics_metrics.description: “The simple statement of the policy is if it’s an error of fact we should fix it and do a correction.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If something published is factually wrong, the newsroom should issue a correction. Examples include wrong names, dates, places, or numeric facts. Corrections are the standard remedy for discrete factual mistakes; frequent small corrections are evidence of institutional dedication to accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use editor’s note for complex news-judgment or fairness issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex cases—such as not calling someone for a response or leaving readers with a misleading impression—may be handled with an editor’s note rather than a standard correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor’s notes are appropriate when the issue involves news judgment, framing, fairness, or other matters that don’t fit the simple factual-error rubric. Examples cited include the Tom Cotton op-ed decision, the 1619 Project historians' objections, and removal of an unfounded anecdote from a first-person essay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of corrections and editor’s notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrections and editor’s notes should be issued promptly; delays of days, weeks, or months undermine reader trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents multiple cases (e.g., Glenn Kessler’s criticisms, Rubio story, Callimachi coverage) where long delays in acknowledging substantive problems caused frustration. Newsrooms should strive to correct or note issues as soon as they can be verified rather than waiting extended periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about who reported the error and how it was handled
rubrics_metrics.description: When issuing a correction or note, disclose if and how the error was brought to the paper’s attention (for example: 'brought to the attention of The Times by a tweet from Glenn Kessler').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicly acknowledging the source of the correction (and the steps taken to verify or fix it) helps accountability. The newsroom should also publicize corrections when appropriate so readers know an error was addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and sufficiency of corrections (avoid overly narrow fixes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrections should address the substantive problem, not only a narrow factual element that leaves the broader misleading impression intact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article criticizes changes that only alter a date or small detail while the article’s larger narrative continues to propagate the error. Corrections should be scoped to remove or clearly qualify any consequential misinformation, and not merely tweak peripheral details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicize corrections when made
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrections should be publicized so readers are aware that an error was corrected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond placing a correction note on the article, the newsroom should make reasonable efforts to call attention to substantive corrections publicly. The Times spokesman’s statement that they 'publicized the correction' is presented as a positive practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous vetting and authentication of documents and sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Before relying on documents or unique sources, verify authenticity and provenance; consult multiple experts when credibility is in doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Callimachi/ISIS receipts case is used as an example where dates and provenance were contested and experts disagreed; initial reporting should not present contested documents as definitive without thorough vetting. If later evidence undermines source authenticity, the reporting and corrections should reflect that shift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable responsiveness to criticism regardless of complainant prominence
rubrics_metrics.description: A newsroom should be receptive to credible error reports from all sources, not only commentators with large platforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece notes that if a high-profile fact-checker waited weeks for a correction, smaller readers will face even greater difficulty. Processes should ensure error reports from less prominent individuals are monitored and acted upon appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek responses from subjects to ensure fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting on people or organizations, the newsroom should attempt to contact them for response as part of fair reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to call someone for comment can create fairness issues that may later require an editor’s note; such failures are harder to categorize as simple factual errors but are still remediable editorially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require specificity from complainants who assert 'all wrong'
rubrics_metrics.description: When a reader asserts that a story is 'all wrong,' editors should ask for specific examples of errors rather than act on a general dismissal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors need concrete points to investigate. The article quotes Corbett noting that vague complaints force editors to distinguish between dislike of a premise and actual factual or fairness errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designated corrections process and reporting channel
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a clear, monitored channel for readers to report errors (example: nytnews@nytimes.com) that is checked by standards/corrections editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having a publicized, monitored email address or form speeds error reporting and ensures corrections editors see and triage issues. The Times’ standards editor and corrections editor personally check the cited address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide clearly between recasting the original story and publishing a new explanatory piece
rubrics_metrics.description: When significant criticism emerges, editors must choose whether to recast the original article or publish a new story and use an editor’s note to direct readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Times opted in one case to publish a new story and place an editor’s note atop the original to explain the dispute and link to the new piece; editors should make a defensible choice that gives readers the clearest account possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid saving face—ensure corrections reflect evolving expert consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: If experts later conclude that source material was inauthentic or reporting was fundamentally flawed, corrections and edits should fully reflect that evolution rather than preserving earlier, more favorable language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Callimachi episode shows a risk where the original article retained language that implied authenticity even after experts revised their judgement; corrections should update or contextualize legacy text so readers are not left with an inaccurate impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a punctilious corrections practice to preserve reader trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular, precise corrections—even of small details—signal an institutional commitment to accuracy and help maintain credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Corrections column’s frequent fine-grained items (name spellings, river names, numerical counts) are presented as a positive pattern that bolsters trust, though the paper should apply the same rigor to larger, substantive issues.
